title: TP-Link tries to appease Trump admin with pledge to assemble routers in US
gist: TP-Link pledged a nearly $1 billion US investment and Mississippi assembly of Wi-Fi 8 routers from 2027 to win FCC exemption from a ban on foreign-made consumer routers, but faces national-security review, state AG lawsuits and no published local-content threshold.

insights.claim: TP-Link proposed a nearly $1 billion US investment and a Letter of Intent with Keytronic to assemble Wi-Fi 8 routers in Corinth, Mississippi from as early as 2027, contingent on regulatory approval.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The investment is conditional, so it works as a bargaining chip, not committed capex.

insights.claim: There is no published guidance on how much US manufacturing is enough for an FCC exemption, and TP-Link says many components are unavailable domestically, a problem for all manufacturers.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Opaque thresholds make onshoring investment risky and reinforce component dependence on China-linked supply chains.
insights.quote: “There are no published guidelines that say, ‘Well, it could be 25 percent US, or it could be 15 percent US,'”
insights.locator: What counts as a US router is unclear

insights.claim: Assembly would still import components, and TP-Link's current devices are made in Vietnam with mostly Chinese-sourced parts, so the plan does not change the supply-chain dependency.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: Regulators may judge on provenance of components, which limits what US assembly achieves.

insights.claim: The FCC bans new consumer routers produced wholly or partly abroad unless exempted, and exemptions require a Department of Defense or Homeland Security finding of no national-security risk; Netgear, Asus, Amazon Eero, Starlink and others have received exemptions.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The ban acts as a de facto licensing regime that advantages incumbents already cleared and shapes home networking market share.
insights.locator: TP-Link struggles to convince Trump admin

insights.claim: TP-Link faces a lawsuit from Florida, Montana, Iowa and Nebraska attorneys general, and a letter from 21 Republican AGs urging the FCC to require remedies and protect users from the Chinese Communist Party.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: State-level litigation adds a parallel track that federal approval alone may not resolve.
insights.locator: Republican AGs urge FCC to stand firm

insights.claim: TP-Link's 2024 move of its HQ to California came amid investigations of Chinese-linked botnets of TP-Link routers, and US intelligence said in April 2026 that Russia's GRU compromised TP-Link routers.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: The security record, not just ownership, is the obstacle to approval.

insights.claim: Router security problems are industry-wide: AirSnitch attacks were reported to work on Netgear, D-Link, Ubiquiti, Cisco and DD-WRT/OpenWrt devices.
insights.speaker: Jon Brodkin
insights.so_what: TP-Link argues for consistent standards; selective enforcement based on origin rather than security posture is its implicit claim.
